Oil Isn’t Balanced, It’s Rerouted: Chokepoints, California, the East Coast and the Case for Home-Grown Energy

Crude Oil Crude Oil News ENB Publisher Picks Energy Crisis Exploration and Production Exports Geopolitical Geopolitical Imports International News Top News U.S. Energy News US Energy News
November 27, 2026 Clark Savage 1
A post on X says Aramco and Vitol both warned of $200 oil. They did, in October, and with conditions attached. We tested my thesis that the world, and states like California and those on the East Coast, need energy that can’t be choked off.
A post on X Friday said Aramco and Vitol, the biggest oil company and biggest oil trader, both warned in the same week that crude would be at $200 without the 13 to 14 million barrels a day still coming out of the Middle East. We checked.

...

The IEA’s table lists effective spare capacity of just 450,000 barrels a day across OPEC+, with none listed for Saudi Arabia, Iraq or Kuwait, though their capacity exceeds October output.
The other side: the IEA also sees “tentative signs of rebalancing”: supply passed demand in October and observed stocks rose 52 million barrels as oil on tankers jumped 86 million. The IEA and the U.S. Energy Information Administration both project a 2027 surplus near 4 million barrels a day, as ENB reported Nov. 25 in Crude Heads for a 2027 Glut, Yet Diesel Stays Tight . EIA’s path to $77 Brent in late 2027 assumes most Middle East output outside Iran returns by mid-2027. That balance is a forecast that depends on open chokepoints.
Chart 1. Oil through major chokepoints, first half 2025 (EIA), and Hormuz in late November 2026 (Kpler, preliminary, different definitions).
Who Gets Squeezed
Before the war, about 20.9 million barrels a day moved through Hormuz, roughly a fifth of world oil use, and 84% of its crude went to Asia, EIA says. U.N. trade data for 2025 show 94% of Japan’s crude imports by value came from the Gulf, 69% of South Korea’s, 48% of India’s and 44% of China’s, against 9% for the United States.
Importers are adapting. Japan’s IEA stock cover fell from 201 days of net imports in February to 176 in August, IEA data cited by Newsbase show. Japan restarted a Kashiwazaki-Kariwa reactor that its economy minister said would save about 30% of the LNG it imports through Hormuz. China and India are on track for record Russian oil imports, averaging 3.4 million barrels a day by sea through mid-November, Vortexa data show. Europe cut Russian gas from 44% of its imports in 2021 to 13% in 2025, a Federal Reserve staff note found, but U.S. cargoes now supply 62% of its LNG, one dependence traded for another.
Chart 2. Gulf share of crude oil imports by value, 2025. Source: UN Comtrade via Apolika.
The Bypass Lesson
Producers that built around chokepoints did better. Saudi Arabia’s energy minister said the East-West line was back to 5.8 million barrels a day on Oct. 6, weeks after a drone attack. The UAE’s Habshan-Fujairah line ran above its 1.5 million barrel nameplate in May, Argus reported. Iraq restarted its old Kirkuk-Ceyhan line Nov. 17 after 12 years and on Friday opened a 300,000 barrel-a-day first phase, Shafaq News reported. The U.S., Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana are adding 1.6 million barrels a day this year, the IEA says, and the U.S. was a net petroleum exporter of about 3.6 million barrels a day in the week to Nov. 20, EIA weekly data show. Nasser, arguing that Middle East supply will stay central, put it this way: “Markets can diversify suppliers. They cannot diversify geology.”
California and the East Coast
California makes about a quarter of the energy it uses, EIA state data show.

...

Risks run both ways: peace or a 2027 surplus could compress prices, margins and freight quickly.
Caveats
The state ratio counts all energy on a Btu basis and excludes federal offshore output. Price gaps also reflect taxes, fuel rules, climate programs, wages and utility costs.
Stu’s Take
We like facts, and the facts say this oil market is balanced only on a spreadsheet.

...

Not every penny is imports, but none of it buys security. Energy you produce at home is energy nobody can choke off.

About this report

The IEA Oil Market Report (OMR) is one of the world's most authoritative and timely sources of data, forecasts and analysis on the global oil market – including detailed statistics and commentary on oil supply, demand, inventories, prices and refining activity, as well as oil trade for IEA and selected non-IEA countries.

Highlights

...

* North Sea Dated crude oil prices tumbled by 32%, dropping from a high of $136/bbl in early October to $93/bbl at the time of writing, as a sustained recovery in Gulf exports eased market tightness. Diesel prices also fell by 11% in Europe over the same period but, at close to $180/bbl, remained 77% above pre-war levels. Freight rates for moving crude from the Middle East to Asia held near record levels, while the costs of Aframaxes and Suezmaxes eased.

Straightening out

...

The higher export rates resulted in a significant uplift to our expectations for global oil supply for the remainder of the year, with 4Q26 estimates raised by 3.3 mb/d. The fourth quarter rebound helped trim the average annual 2026 decline to 4.8 mb/d, with losses from the Middle East and Russia partly offset by growth from producers outside the Gulf. Notably, the Americas Quintet – the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana – are on track to boost output by 1.6 mb/d this year. In 2027, global supply is projected to recover by 6.6 mb/d to 108.1 mb/d, including a 5.3 mb/d increase in Gulf production and a further 1.1 mb/d gain from the Quintet.

...

Our November supply and demand balances suggest that the global oil market will return to a surplus in 4Q26, with a more substantial build in 2027. As always, downside risks to the forecast persist, as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery.
For now, the severe tightness in product supply, especially for diesel, remains the overriding concern of the broader market and consumers. Persistent attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to choke off the country’s diesel supplies to international markets, adding to losses from the Middle East. At the same time, Atlantic Basin refineries, particularly in the United States, are running hard to capture high margins, while improved crude availability in Asia and fresh Chinese product export quotas could support higher refinery throughput rates in the region. Notably, the accelerated release of IEA emergency diesel stocks over the coming months will provide a critical bridge across the supply gap until the global refinery system and product output recover.

Mideast Gulf crude discounts deepen as Asian refiners turn to Atlantic barrels

Ample Middle East crude supplies and falling tanker rates are reshaping competition for Asian refinery demand.
* Dubai's prompt premium collapses : Dubai M1–M3 narrowed from +$11.03/bbl on 6 October to +$1.03/bbl on 12 November, approaching contango as Middle East crude supply availability improves. Saudi Arabia and Kuwait have cut December OSPs by $2/bbl, intensifying competition to defend market share in Asia.

Source : Kpler (derived from market sources)
* Atlantic crude attracts Asian buyers : Chinese refiners are stepping up purchases of West African and Brazilian crude despite cheaper Middle Eastern alternatives. Kpler assessments show Agbami's landed value into Ningbo falling $11.95/bbl w/w to +$19.65/bbl versus Dubai Swap for late-November loading. At current levels, prompt Agbami cargoes are around $4/bbl more competitive than Murban, strengthening the incentive for Asian refiners to source West African barrels.
* WAF differentials set to strengthen : We expect improving eastbound economics and renewed Asian buying interest to support West African crude differentials, particularly as falling freight gives sellers room to capture some of the delivered-price advantage. However, further Gulf OSP reductions could erode that competitiveness and limit the upside.

candidates.snippet:
Europe is building drone defenses. But can it make them work together?

European governments are spending billions to protect their skies. Turning those national investments into a coherent defense capability may prove more difficult.
Illustrative image of a soldier retrieving an Anafi USA drone during a live-fire exercise at Novo Selo Training Area, Bulgaria, 7 August 2025. (J Marshall/Tribaleye Images)
By Paula Soler
Paula Soler is a reporter at The Parliament Magazine
25 Nov 2026
@pausoler98
Share this page
   ?subject=Europe+is+building+drone+defenses.+But+can+it+make+them+work+together%3f&body=theparliamentmagazine.eu%2fnews%2farticle%2feurope-is-building-drone-defenses-but-can-it-make-them-work-together 
Europe's skies have become increasingly difficult to defend. Drones have disrupted airports, appeared over military installations and exposed weaknesses in air defenses designed for a different era. At least 144 drone incidents were reported across the European Union between August 2024 and February 2026, according to a report from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In response, Brussels put forward plans for a "drone wall" in 2025. A year later, the rebranded European Drone Defence Initiative , the multilayered system for detecting, neutralizing and striking dronesis due to reach initial capacity by the end of December and become fully operational a year later.
Much of the work is taking place at the national level.

...

Turning innovation into contracts

Europe's drone industry has a familiar defense problem: demand for its products is soaring, but orders are not coming fast enough.
EU countries plan to invest €18.9 billion in drone technologies between 2024 and 2029, according to a leaked report by the European Defence Agency . Yet only a third of planned counter-drone and very short-range air defense programs are expected to be delivered by the end of the decade.
In an industry where technology can become obsolete within months, Europe's lengthy procurement procedures risk leaving armed forces with equipment that is already outdated by the time it enters service.
"Procurement is not materializing at a pace that matches the urgency," said Arthur de Liedekerke, a partner and senior director at political consultancy Rasmussen Global.
The government departments responsible for buying military equipment have not necessarily expanded alongside defense budgets, he said, while decades of working with established manufacturers have made it difficult for smaller, more innovative companies to break into the market.
"We need shorter procurement cycles, operational testing with end users and contracts that allow frequent upgrades," he said.
Some manufacturers are already benefiting from Europe's military spending spree.

...

But governments that develop their drone defenses in isolation risk investing in overlapping technologies, deploying systems that cannot exchange data and creating legal uncertainty over when and by whom drones can be intercepted, defense experts say.
“To ensure coherence and interoperability, especially at the data-exchange level, more coordination needs to happen now,” Ulrike Franke, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, a pan-European think tank, wrote in an August analysis .
There is also the question of how much Europe can afford to spend defending its skies.

...

Where national interests collide

Disagreements over what constitutes the bigger threat make protecting European airspace even harder.
For governments on NATO's eastern flank, drones are part of a broader military threat from Russia. Further west, much of the concern centers on how vulnerable airports, ports and other sensitive sites are to disruption, espionage and sabotage.

EDA says six EU countries explore joint purchase of CBRN surveillance equipment and services

By Defence Industry Europe (newsroom)
EU | November 21, 2026
EDA says six EU countries explore joint purchase of CBRN surveillance equipment and services
Photo: European Defence Agency (EDA).
Austria, Croatia, Germany, Lithuania, Slovakia and Slovenia are exploring a joint purchase of chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear surveillance equipment and services, the European Defence Agency said. Any procurement would remain subject to national approval procedures.
The six countries signed a declaration of political intent on 17 November 2026 alongside EDA’s Ministerial Steering Board meeting. It opens the way to possible common procurement under the next phase of the CBRN Surveillance as a Service project, with development expected to finish in mid-2027.
EDA’s new Collaborative Defence Procurement Centre, or CDPC, will support the initiative by helping the countries combine requirements and coordinate purchases. Other EU member states will be invited to take part.
“European defence readiness requires more than ambition. It requires delivering concrete capabilities together,” said EDA Chief Executive André Denk.
“Through its new Collaborative Defence Procurement Centre, EDA can help Member States combine their purchasing power, coordinate joint procurement, reduce costs and deliver interoperable solutions. This is how EDA turns European defence cooperation into concrete results,” Denk said.
Austria leads the project, which builds on cooperation launched in 2018 under Permanent Structured Cooperation, or PESCO, with EDA support. National experts, innovators and industry have worked together on technologies intended to improve CBRN reconnaissance and surveillance.
These include sensors that detect hazardous chemical, biological and radiological substances and transmit information about them. Mounted on drones or autonomous ground vehicles, the sensors allow forces to investigate threats while reducing the risk of exposing personnel.
Specially developed software immediately processes the transmitted data and produces a real-time CBRN situational picture to support commanders’ decisions. Some of the technologies were recently tested during the EU Operational Experimentation exercise in Portugal, demonstrating their potential for operational use.
“The countries that acquire the CBRN reconnaissance and surveillance systems under this project can easily cooperate with the systems of other participating countries. Threats can be detected without putting human lives at risk,” said Austrian Defence Minister Klaudia Tanner.
The declaration follows defence ministers’ September 2026 approval of a stronger EDA role in capability development, innovation and collaborative procurement. That decision included establishing the CDPC to help governments pool requirements and buy services and off-the-shelf solutions together.
The planned purchase would give participants interoperable systems and services, with combined demand offering economies of scale and a lower administrative burden. EDA said the initiative illustrated how collaborative development could lead to joint acquisition, supporting the broader objective of European defence readiness by 2030.
Source: European Defence Agency (press release) .

European Defence Agency says EU ministers endorsed eight cooperation opportunities spanning missiles and strategic enablers

By Martin Chomsky (Defence Industry Europe)
EU | November 23, 2026
European Defence Agency says EU ministers endorsed eight cooperation opportunities spanning missiles and strategic enablers
Photo: European Defence Agency (EDA).
EU defence ministers have endorsed eight opportunities for military cooperation in a review that urges governments to plan capabilities together before taking national procurement decisions. The 2026 Coordinated Annual Review on Defence (CARD), approved on 17 November, identifies opportunities ranging from missiles and unmanned systems to the infrastructure needed to sustain European operations.
The report finds that agreement on defence priorities has not yet translated into a consistently collaborative approach to purchasing equipment. It recommends considering cooperation at the capability planning stage and incorporating it into national programmes and budgets, with projects prepared to draw on EU funding.
Ministers endorsed opportunities to cooperate on a family of cruise missiles, long-range artillery using multiple launch rocket systems and a family of long-range air defence interceptors. They also backed opportunities involving modular, interoperable unmanned ground vehicles and layered counter-drone systems for force protection and critical infrastructure.
The other three opportunities concern space-based early warning, detection and tracking, a European secure defence cloud and a European approach to strategic air mobility. The European Defence Agency (EDA) identifies these as strategic enablers that allow Europe to decide, act and sustain operations autonomously.
“With CARD, we have identified three collaborative opportunities related to strategic enablers,” said EDA Chief Executive André Denk. “From space-based early warning to strategic air mobility, and a secure, federated defence cloud architecture, these strategic enablers are essential to strengthening Europe’s deterrence and defence capabilities.”
Their scale, cost and dependence on shared architectures and networks make cooperation necessary, the report says. It argues that no single country can develop and support them alone, while access cannot be assumed in every future contingency.
CARD calls for further analysis, stronger member-state involvement and dedicated roadmaps for these capabilities. That work should build on EDA’s activities and Priority Capability Areas, in coherence with NATO.
The report makes five recommendations covering earlier cooperation, planning beyond 2030, joint work on strategic enablers, the full process of capability development and faster adoption of innovation. It stresses that buying equipment is only part of delivering forces that can deploy and operate effectively.
Personnel, training, doctrine, logistics, sustainment and interoperability increasingly determine how much defence investment becomes usable capability. Shared training capacity, common information-sharing architectures and integration of sensors with command and control offer opportunities that can be delivered faster than large programmes.
The review also identifies delays between promising technological results and operational use. It attributes those delays to experimentation, requirements and acquisition being managed too sequentially and calls for innovation to reach the field faster.
Immediate readiness requirements must be balanced with investment in medium- and long-term needs beyond 2030. The report warns that underinvestment may become visible only after several planning cycles, when correcting it would take considerable time and money.
More systematic cooperation would give manufacturers clearer and more predictable demand, supporting production at scale and reducing supply-chain dependencies. Delivering that cooperation also requires stronger intergovernmental support for joint acquisition, capability development and research.
EDA’s strengthening process is intended to provide that support and help CARD and Permanent Structured Cooperation (PESCO) deliver results. EU incentives, including the European Defence Industry Programme, would support those efforts.
At the 17 November EDA Steering Board, ministers also endorsed a joint statement on defence security of supply. They agreed to increase the agency’s budget.
EDA prepared the report in coordination with the European External Action Service and the EU Military Staff. It is the final deliverable of the fourth CARD cycle, covering 2025–2026.

candidates.source_name: European Air and Missile Defence: Who Is Buying What (ESSI, IRIS-T, Patriot, Arrow 3, SAMP/T, Skyranger)
candidates.snippet:
TL;DR: As of 7 November 2026, Europe's air-defence buildout runs on three tracks at once: a standardised medium tier built on Diehl's IRIS-T SLM under the European Sky Shield Initiative, ordered by Bulgaria at EUR 1.1 billion; an upper tier still entirely non-European (Israeli Arrow 3, American Patriot) whose rounds are rationed between allied stocks, Germany's two replacement fire units and Ukraine's 500 PAC-3 MSE, notified on 30 October with no delivery date; and a widening field of alternatives — France's SAMP/T NG fleet raised to twelve sections, Switzerland's choice between SAMP/T NG and Barak MX, Greece's Israeli Achilles Shield at EUR 3.035 billion — that ESSI's own menu does not cover.

...

Who's moving — France ordered four more SAMP/T NG sections on 21 October, twelve in all, ten by end-2030; Germany's procurement office ordered its two replacement Patriot fire units on 2 November; Bulgaria's government approved 32 naval surface-to-air missiles through a French–Danish joint buy on 28 October; Kongsberg signed NOK 10 billion of NASAMS for Belgium on 29 September.
Open question — Switzerland narrowed its second long-range system to SAMP/T NG or Barak MX on 28 October and kept its slipped Patriot order; parliament takes the CHF 24 billion army-financing bill, with CHF 6 billion for the second system, and the CHF 970 million advance-payment credit in the winter session, and the Federal Council's next step is expected in early 2027.
State of play · Key numbers · The ledger · What to watch · Related

Background

European air-and-missile-defence procurement now runs across a dozen simultaneous national tracks — ESSI members buying IRIS-T SLM and Patriot, France and Italy expanding SAMP/T NG, Germany building three interceptor tiers at once, Switzerland and Greece stepping outside the standard menu entirely, and Ukraine's winter now bargained for out of the same Patriot stocks and production slots.
Whether a given capital's air defence arrives in 2027 or 2031 depends on contract values, delivery dates and a handful of production bottlenecks — above all the US solid-rocket-motor line — that no government publishes side by side.

State of play

The ESSI buyer map

The European Sky Shield Initiative, proposed by Germany in August 2022, has grown to roughly two dozen signatories from the Arctic to the Mediterranean, including neutral Austria and Switzerland.

...

The NASAMS tier of the menu moved too: Kongsberg signed NOK 10 billion for Belgium on 29 September, through the Dutch procurement agency.
France, Italy, Spain and Poland have stayed out. Paris's objection is structural: ESSI leans on non-European hardware and left the Franco-Italian SAMP/T off the original menu, undercutting the strategic-autonomy case Paris makes for its own system. That fault line — not a Europe-versus-NATO split — is the one that actually runs through the continent's air-defence procurement, and it shapes almost every purchase that follows.

Patriot's bottleneck, and who is queue-jumping it

The constraint on PAC-3 MSE was never final assembly at Lockheed's Camden, Arkansas line — it is the solid rocket motor.

...

Key numbers

* Metric | Value | As of | Source
* ESSI membership | ~24 states | 14 Jul 2026 | ESSI participating-ministry statements (BMVg and signatory defence ministries)
* IRIS-T SLM signed ESSI operators | 8 states (Germany, Estonia, Latvia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Switzerland, Sweden, Denmark) | 31 May 2026 | Diehl Defence order announcements
* IRIS-T SLM combined order pipeline | >€5 billion | 21 Feb 2026 | Diehl Defence contract announcements, aggregated

...

The ledger

2 Nov 2026 Signal No. 180
The Bundeswehr's procurement office announces the order of two Patriot fire units with services and spare-parts packages, replacing the two Germany gave Ukraine, together with containerised maintenance facilities that replace late-1980s equipment; the budget committee had approved both on 14 October, the fire units at about EUR 650 million through Foreign Military Sales.

...

The contrarian read

The prevailing reading is that ESSI and its IRIS-T SLM anchor are converging Europe on a shared medium-tier standard while the upper tier catches up. The harder read is that convergence is not what is happening at all. Greece signed for €3.035 billion on 31 August 2026 to put its national shield entirely outside the Patriot/SAMP-T frame, on Israeli sensors and interceptors; Switzerland has narrowed its second long-range system to the Franco-Italian SAMP/T NG and Israel's Barak MX while keeping a Patriot order it says it cannot drop without an alternative; and three separate corporate command-and-control architectures — Thales's SkyDefender, Leonardo's Michelangelo, Rheinmetall's Electronic Solutions — are competing to become the integration layer no single government has chosen yet.

Sovereignty is here to stay in space defence spending

November 2026

Alexander Clark

Governments worldwide are increasing their spending on space-based defence capabilities as geopolitical fragmentation forces them to seek sovereign control over their assets. NATO members and partner countries 1 have awarded over USD51 billion in total contract value on space-based defence in 2026, up from USD20 billion in 2025. 2 Early investment this year included procurement of satellite communications (satcom) and Earth observation satellites for secure, reliable access to data and networks. However, the largest portion of spending has gone to missile early warning (MEW) and space domain awareness (SDA) as governments and militaries work to expand monitoring capabilities and increasingly leverage space for defence purposes.
Sovereignty will remain a dominant theme in space spending through 2027 and beyond, and this presents an opportunity for vendors selling in national markets. 3 However, the trend will challenge vendors seeking to sell internationally, especially given changes in government, delays in space defence programmes and distinct national preferences.

Saipem Bags $650M in Aramco Deals Covering Five Offshore Fields

Published Nov 25, 2026 4:57 am ET
(Credit: Saipem)
(Credit: Saipem)
Saipem has secured two offshore engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) contracts from Aramco in Saudi Arabia worth approximately $650 million, covering production deck manifolds, pipelines, power cables and associated subsea infrastructure.
The awards, designated Contract Release Purchase Orders (CRPOs) 168 and 170, fall under Saipem's existing Long-Term Agreement with Aramco.
The first contract, CRPO 168, covers the EPCI of four production deck manifolds (PDMs), approximately 14 kilometers of pipelines with diameters ranging from 12 to 16 inches, and around 24 kilometers of 15 kV power cables.
The scope also includes associated subsea facilities serving the Abu Safah, Safaniyah, Manifa and Berri fields, alongside onshore tie-in activities at the drill site in the Manifa field.
